# The Coat

The woman arrived on a Tuesday, which was unusual. Most of my customers came on Saturdays, when they had time to stand in front of the mirror and deliberate. She came at ten in the morning with a garment bag folded over her arm like something she was ashamed of.

"I need a coat taken in," she said. "Significantly."

I took the bag from her and unzipped it at the counter. The coat was charcoal wool, good quality once, but the shoulders had gone shiny with age and the lining at the collar was worn through to the canvas. It was a man's coat. A tall man's.

"It's not mine," she said, before I could ask.

I lifted it out. The label inside was from a shop in Leeds that had closed years ago. There was a repair on the left cuff, done by hand, done well—not by a professional, but by someone patient. I recognized the stitch. My mother used it.

"Can you hold it up?" she asked. "I want to see it."

I held it against the light from the window. The coat had been well cared for and then not cared for at all. The last few years of its life had been hard ones.
